chapterTitle: UI Basics: Canvas, Rect Transforms & UI Elements
aiGenerationNote: Create a 10-minute interactive lab walkthrough video. Begin by creating a new Unity scene. Demonstrate creating a Canvas and explaining its three render modes with visual examples (overlay for HUD, camera for specific camera effects, world space for in-game objects like character health bars). Then, focus on Rect Transforms: show how to create a TextMeshPro title and an Image background. Manipulate anchors (corner vs. stretch) and pivots in the Scene view, explaining their impact on responsiveness. Add a Button and explain its basic properties. Include a split-screen view of the Inspector and Scene view, dynamically resizing the Game window to show UI responsiveness. Conclude with a mini-quiz asking about the best anchor settings for a specific UI element. Emphasize visual clarity and hands-on manipulation.

screens.title: Canvas, Rect Transforms & UI Elements
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn the three core pieces you’ll use to build game interfaces: the Canvas, Rect Transform, and the basic UI elements like TextMeshPro, Image, and Button. The Canvas is the drawing surface that must contain all UGUI objects; choosing the right render mode—overlay, camera, or world space—determines whether the UI floats above the scene, is drawn by a specific camera, or behaves like a 3D object. Rect Transform replaces the normal Transform for UI elements and uses anchors, pivots, and offsets so that UI responds to different screen sizes. We’ll also create a simple main menu with a title, background image, and a start button to demonstrate responsiveness and hierarchy. Understanding how render mode, anchoring, and sibling order interact prevents common problems such as invisible text or misplaced buttons. By the end, you will be able to select a Canvas mode for a use case, position a UI element with anchors and pivots, and assemble a working button with a TextMeshPro label. Think about a health bar above a moving enemy—pick a render mode that keeps it visually attached. Ready to explore the pieces and how they fit together?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the practical skills you’ll practice in the lab. First, you will clearly explain what a Canvas does and choose the appropriate render mode for a given UI need. For example, deciding between overlay for HUDs or world space for in-game labels is a frequent design choice. Second, you will understand how Rect Transform anchors, pivots, and offsets work together to position and size UI across resolutions. You’ll practice setting corner and stretch anchors and see how offsets change when anchors move. Third, you will create and configure basic UI elements: a TextMeshPro title for crisp text, an Image for background or iconography, and a Button wired to an OnClick event to trigger actions. Finally, you will diagnose common hierarchy and rendering order problems, such as elements hiding behind others or TextMeshPro failing to render because resources were not imported. Each objective ties to a small hands-on step so you can verify competency and build a responsive main menu. These skills matter because clean, responsive interfaces directly affect player experience and usability.

screens.title: Canvas: the UI drawing surface
screens.narratorSegment: A Canvas is the root GameObject that Unity’s UGUI system uses as the drawing surface for all UI elements. In practical terms, if you create a TextMeshPro, Image, or Button, Unity will create a Canvas automatically when none exists. The Canvas manages how and when child UI elements are batched and rendered, and its render mode determines whether the UI sits on top of the scene, is drawn by a specific camera, or becomes a 3D object within the world. A concrete example: a pause menu that must always appear above gameplay should use Screen Space - Overlay so it ignores scene depth and always shows. A common misconception is thinking a Canvas is merely a parent for organization; instead it also controls sorting, scaling, and event handling through its settings. If you nest many canvases, be aware each one can introduce separate batching behaviour and sorting changes, so use multiple canvases only when needed for performance or distinct render behavior. Key takeaway: without a correctly configured Canvas you cannot display or reliably control UI layout and input. Canvas: the UI drawing surface means canvas is the required root for ugui; render mode decides overlay, camera-drawn, or in-world ui behavior.. In practical terms, what the canvas is and why every ugui element needs one. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Canvas
Canvas: the UI drawing surface
The required root GameObject for all UGUI elements and the place render mode is set.
Definition & role
  • Manages draw order, scaling, and event routing for child UI.
  • Automatically created when adding your first UI element.
  • Render Mode controls overlay, camera rendering, or world placement.
Key Takeaway
Configure the Canvas render mode to match your use case; it directly affects how UI is drawn and interacted with.
Example scenarios
HUD or Pause Menu
Use Screen Space - Overlay so UI always appears above gameplay.
Camera-specific UI
Use Screen Space - Camera when you want to apply camera effects to UI or target one camera.
In-world UI (health bar)
Use World Space when UI must occupy a position in 3D space and be occluded by objects.
Common mistake: treating Canvas as just a container. It controls rendering and input behavior.

screens.title: Canvas Render Modes
screens.narratorSegment: There are three Canvas render modes and each fits a clear purpose. Screen Space - Overlay renders UI directly on top of all scene content; it scales to the screen and ignores 3D depth. Use it for HUDs and menus that must always be visible. Screen Space - Camera renders UI through a specified camera, letting you control render order relative to other camera effects and enabling per-camera UI layers. Use this when multiple cameras require distinct UI or when post-processing should affect UI. World Space treats UI as a 3D object with position, rotation, and scale inside the scene. Use it for in-world labels, interactive panels, or health bars that must move with a character and be occluded by scene geometry. A concrete example: attach a small world-space Canvas to an enemy for a floating health bar so it moves with the enemy and can be hidden behind walls. A common misconception is assuming world-space UI will automatically scale well on all displays—when used in world space you must set physical sizes and consider distance-based scaling or billboard techniques. Question to reflect on: which mode ensures UI receives input from a specific camera?

keyIdea.title: Render mode decision
keyIdea.text: Overlay for always-on UI, Camera for camera-specific rendering, World for in-scene interactive elements.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Canvas Modes
Canvas Render Modes
Choose based on layering, camera effects, and whether UI sits in the world.
Screen Space - Overlay
Always-on HUDs and menus
Renders on top of scene, auto-scales to screen, simple and common for menus.
Misconception: overlay blocks interaction with scene objects—UI only receives input if you set up events.
Screen Space - Camera
Camera-specific UI
Rendered by a chosen camera; useful for multi-camera setups or when camera post-processing should affect UI.
Practical note: assign the Render Camera in the Canvas to control which camera draws the UI.
World Space
In-scene UI objects
UI behaves like a 3D object and can be occluded or moved with GameObjects in the scene.
Misconception: world-space UI does not auto-scale for resolution; you must design for physical size and distance.
Concrete example
Attach a small world-space Canvas to an enemy for a health bar so it moves and can be occluded. Use overlay for your main HUD and camera mode for a picture-in-picture camera with its own UI.

screens.title: Rect Transform: anchors, pivots, and offsets
screens.narratorSegment: Rect Transform is a specialized Transform for Unity UI that defines a rectangular area and how it behaves relative to its parent. Unlike a normal Transform, it exposes anchors, pivot, and offset fields that determine position and size in 2D. Anchors are reference points on the parent rect—set both anchors to a single point to fix the element to a corner, or stretch anchors across the parent to make the child resize with the parent. The pivot is the local origin for rotation and scaling; a pivot of center means rotation happens around the center, while a corner pivot rotates from that corner. Offsets change meaning depending on anchors: when anchors are together, Pos X and Pos Y are offsets from the anchor; when anchors stretch, Left/Right/Top/Bottom represent padding from parent edges. A concrete example: to keep a title centered, set anchors to middle-center; to create a full-screen background, set anchors to stretch-stretch and zero out offsets. A common mistake is setting anchors incorrectly and wondering why an element doesn’t scale—anchors drive responsiveness, not just position. Try resizing the Game view while adjusting anchors to build intuition.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Rect Transform
Rect Transform: anchors, pivots, and offsets
Understand how UI elements maintain placement and scale across screen sizes.
Core pieces
  • Anchors: reference points on the parent rect that determine how the child positions or stretches.
  • Pivot: local origin for rotation and scale, expressed in normalized coordinates.
  • Offsets/Pos: positional values that change meaning when anchors are set to stretch.
Tip: use the anchor presets in the Inspector to quickly apply corner or stretch behavior.
Concrete example
Centered Title
Set anchors to middle-center and pivot to (0.5,0.5). Pos X and Pos Y become offsets from the center, keeping the title centered on different screens.
Full-screen Background
Set anchors to stretch-stretch and set Left/Right/Top/Bottom to zero to fill the parent rect.
Common mistake: changing Pos values with stretch anchors active rather than adjusting padding; understand which properties control what under each anchor mode.

screens.title: Anchors: point vs stretch
screens.narratorSegment: Anchors can be set to a single point or can stretch across the parent. When anchors are a single point—like top-left—the UI element’s Pos X and Pos Y are straight offsets from that anchor. This is ideal for placing a button in a corner with a fixed offset. When anchors stretch across an axis, the element resizes with the parent and Left/Right/Top/Bottom values act as padding. Use stretch anchors to create elements that track parent size, like a responsive background or a progress bar that scales. A concrete example: a health bar across the top should use left and right anchors stretched to both sides, with Top and Bottom offsets to set height. A common misconception is thinking anchors alone will center an element; you often also need to set pivot and Pos values. Another point: when you change anchor positions in the Scene view Unity can optionally keep the current apparent rectangle or update offsets—learn to use the anchored position vs world position presets to avoid unexpected jumps. Takeaway: choose point anchors for fixed offsets and stretch anchors for responsive sizing.

keyIdea.title: Anchor behavior
keyIdea.text: Point anchors keep fixed offsets; stretch anchors make the child scale with parent and use padding values instead of simple position.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Anchors
Anchors: point vs stretch
Pick anchors based on whether the element should hold position or resize with its parent.
Point anchors
Anchors at a single point (corners or center) make Pos X/Pos Y offsets relative to that anchor. Use for elements that should remain at a fixed offset, like a corner button.
Example
Bottom-right button with Pos X -50, Pos Y 50 stays offset from edges regardless of screen size.
Stretch anchors
Anchors stretched across the parent make the child resize with the parent. Left/Right/Top/Bottom become padding values rather than simple position offsets.
Example
Full-width header: anchors stretched left to right with Top and Bottom padding to control height.
Misconception check
Changing anchors can alter offsets. Use the anchor presets with care: choose whether Unity should preserve position or update offsets when you change anchors to avoid surprises.

screens.title: Pivots, Position and Size explained
screens.narratorSegment: The pivot is the local origin point of a UI element’s Rect Transform and is expressed in normalized coordinates where (0,0) is bottom-left and (1,1) is top-right. Rotations and scaling occur around this pivot. For example, if you set the pivot to (0,1) — the top-left corner — and rotate the element, it will pivot around that corner instead of the center. Position and size fields change meaning depending on anchors: with point anchors, Pos X and Pos Y represent the offset from the anchor; with stretch anchors, the size is determined by the parent and Left/Right/Top/Bottom act like padding. A concrete lab example is making a button that grows from its center when hovered: set pivot to (0.5,0.5) and animate scale. A common mistake is rotating around an unexpected point because the pivot was left at a corner; always confirm pivot placement before animating. Closing thought: visualize the pivot like the hinge of a door — it tells you where rotations and scale originate and shapes how layout behaves. Pivots, Position and Size explained means pivot sets the local origin for rotation and scaling; offsets depend on whether anchors are points or stretches.. In practical terms, pivot as rotation origin and how offsets behave. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Pivot & Size
Pivots, Position and Size explained
Pivot determines the rotation and scaling origin; size fields are contextual to anchors.
Pivot as hinge
Pivot (0.5,0.5) centers rotation. Pivot (0,1) rotates around top-left. Always check pivot before animating transforms.
Analogy: pivot is the hinge of a door, not the whole door itself.
Size and offsets
With point anchors: Pos X/Pos Y are offsets. With stretch anchors: Left/Right/Top/Bottom control padding from edges and size changes with parent.
Try this
Switch a background Image to stretch-stretch anchors and set padding to zero to fill its parent. Observe how size fields update automatically.

screens.title: TextMeshPro and Image fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: TextMeshPro is Unity’s recommended text solution for UI because it offers higher quality rendering, richer formatting, and improved performance over the legacy Text component. When you create a Text - TextMeshPro object, the editor will prompt you to import essential resources; if you skip this the text may not render correctly. Use TMP for titles, labels, and any text requiring crisp scaling. Configure font size, alignment, and rich text tags to format content. Images display sprites or textures and are used for backgrounds, icons, and decorative elements. Set the Source Image property to a sprite and choose Image Type such as Simple, Sliced, or Filled. Sliced images are useful for scalable UI panels because they preserve corner radii when stretched. Concrete example: make a large TextMeshPro title with font size around 72, centered via middle-center anchors; add a background Image set to stretch-stretch and a sliced sprite so the panel scales cleanly. A common mistake is leaving TMP resources unimported or using non-sliced sprites for scalable panels, which causes visual distortion when resized. Final takeaway: TMP plus properly sliced images are the backbone of dependable UI visuals.

keyIdea.title: Text & Image
keyIdea.text: Use TextMeshPro for crisp text and sliced Image types for scalable UI panels; import TMP resources to avoid missing text.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Text & Image
TextMeshPro and Image fundamentals
Ensure TMP resources are imported and use sliced images for scalable panels.
TextMeshPro essentials
  • Import TMP essential resources when prompted.
  • Set font size, alignment, and rich text tags for emphasis.
  • Use middle-center anchors for centered titles that respond to resize.
Image component tips
  • Assign a Sprite to Source Image.
  • Use Sliced type for panels that must scale without distorting corners.
  • Fill type is useful for bars and progress indicators.
Concrete example
Create a TextMeshPro GameTitle with font size 72 and center it. Add an Image named Background set to stretch-stretch; use a sliced sprite so it fills screens without corner distortion.

screens.title: Button basics and wiring OnClick
screens.narratorSegment: A Button in Unity is an interactive composite: typically an Image for visuals combined with a Button component that exposes an OnClick event. To create a Start button in the lab, add UI > Button - TextMeshPro. Rename it StartButton and edit its child Text (TMP) to read "Start Game". Place the button with middle-center anchors and a Pos Y offset so it sits beneath the title. Wiring the button: in the Inspector, the Button component’s OnClick list accepts target GameObjects and public methods to call. A concrete example is adding a script with a public method called StartGame and dragging the GameObject into the OnClick slot, then selecting the method. Test in Play mode to ensure clicking triggers the action. A common mistake is forgetting to make the method public or assigning a non-Play mode-only method. Also verify no transparent Image covers the button and prevents clicks. Closing takeaway: Buttons are simple visually, but rely on correct hierarchy, a visible interactive image component, and a public method bound to OnClick to function reliably. Button basics and wiring OnClick means buttons combine image visuals and a button component; bind public methods to onclick and ensure no sibling blocks the clickable area.. Understand sibling index, Canvas nesting, and common visibility issues.
Sibling order rules
Elements render top-to-bottom in Hierarchy. Move a child above another to bring it forward. Use reorder commands or drag in Hierarchy to change drawing order.
Multiple Canvas effects
Separate canvases allow independent sorting and can improve batching performance when changing only parts of the UI. Use them when you need separate sorting layers or frequent updates limited to a region.

In this lesson we will learn the three core pieces you’ll use to build game interfaces: the Canvas, Rect Transform, and the basic UI elements like TextMeshPro, Image, and Button. The Canvas is the drawing surface that must contain all UGUI objects; choosing the right render mode—overlay, camera, or world space—determines whether the UI floats above the scene, is drawn by a specific camera, or behaves like a 3D object. Rect Transform replaces the normal Transform for UI elements and uses anchors, pivots, and offsets so that UI responds to different screen sizes. We’ll also create a simple main menu with a title, background image, and a start button to demonstrate responsiveness and hierarchy. Understanding how render mode, anchoring, and sibling order interact prevents common problems such as invisible text or misplaced buttons. By the end, you will be able to select a Canvas mode for a use case, position a UI element with anchors and pivots, and assemble a working button with a TextMeshPro label. Think about a health bar above a moving enemy—pick a render mode that keeps it visually attached. Ready to explore the pieces and how they fit together?

These objectives guide the practical skills you’ll practice in the lab. First, you will clearly explain what a Canvas does and choose the appropriate render mode for a given UI need. For example, deciding between overlay for HUDs or world space for in-game labels is a frequent design choice. Second, you will understand how Rect Transform anchors, pivots, and offsets work together to position and size UI across resolutions. You’ll practice setting corner and stretch anchors and see how offsets change when anchors move. Third, you will create and configure basic UI elements: a TextMeshPro title for crisp text, an Image for background or iconography, and a Button wired to an OnClick event to trigger actions. Finally, you will diagnose common hierarchy and rendering order problems, such as elements hiding behind others or TextMeshPro failing to render because resources were not imported. Each objective ties to a small hands-on step so you can verify competency and build a responsive main menu. These skills matter because clean, responsive interfaces directly affect player experience and usability.

This page extends the checklist and emphasizes practical checks to run while building UI. You should be able to inspect the Canvas properties and confirm the render mode and the assigned camera, if any. Practice switching the Game view size to validate anchors and stretches. For TextMeshPro, ensure essential resources are imported so text actually appears; this is a frequent oversight. For Buttons, test the OnClick event in Play mode and verify the clickable area is not occluded by other transparent images. When diagnosing a missing UI element, check sibling order, Canvas sorting layers, and whether a parent object’s Rect Transform clamps or masks children. These checks are quick but powerful: they prevent time-consuming layout bugs. Each objective includes a simple mnemonic and a small hands-on verification step you can run in under a minute, reinforcing that UI is both visual and rule-based. By practicing these checks you will move from making one-off menus to building reliable, resolution-safe interfaces.

A Canvas is the root GameObject that Unity’s UGUI system uses as the drawing surface for all UI elements. In practical terms, if you create a TextMeshPro, Image, or Button, Unity will create a Canvas automatically when none exists. The Canvas manages how and when child UI elements are batched and rendered, and its render mode determines whether the UI sits on top of the scene, is drawn by a specific camera, or becomes a 3D object within the world. A concrete example: a pause menu that must always appear above gameplay should use Screen Space - Overlay so it ignores scene depth and always shows. A common misconception is thinking a Canvas is merely a parent for organization; instead it also controls sorting, scaling, and event handling through its settings. If you nest many canvases, be aware each one can introduce separate batching behaviour and sorting changes, so use multiple canvases only when needed for performance or distinct render behavior. Key takeaway: without a correctly configured Canvas you cannot display or reliably control UI layout and input. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. There are three Canvas render modes and each fits a clear purpose. Screen Space - Overlay renders UI directly on top of all scene content; it scales to the screen and ignores 3D depth. Use it for HUDs and menus that must always be visible. Screen Space - Camera renders UI through a specified camera, letting you control render order relative to other camera effects and enabling per-camera UI layers. Use this when multiple cameras require distinct UI or when post-processing should affect UI. World Space treats UI as a 3D object with position, rotation, and scale inside the scene. Use it for in-world labels, interactive panels, or health bars that must move with a character and be occluded by scene geometry. A concrete example: attach a small world-space Canvas to an enemy for a floating health bar so it moves with the enemy and can be hidden behind walls. A common misconception is assuming world-space UI will automatically scale well on all displays—when used in world space you must set physical sizes and consider distance-based scaling or billboard techniques. Question to reflect on: which mode ensures UI receives input from a specific camera?

Rect Transform is a specialized Transform for Unity UI that defines a rectangular area and how it behaves relative to its parent. Unlike a normal Transform, it exposes anchors, pivot, and offset fields that determine position and size in 2D. Anchors are reference points on the parent rect—set both anchors to a single point to fix the element to a corner, or stretch anchors across the parent to make the child resize with the parent. The pivot is the local origin for rotation and scaling; a pivot of center means rotation happens around the center, while a corner pivot rotates from that corner. Offsets change meaning depending on anchors: when anchors are together, Pos X and Pos Y are offsets from the anchor; when anchors stretch, Left/Right/Top/Bottom represent padding from parent edges. A concrete example: to keep a title centered, set anchors to middle-center; to create a full-screen background, set anchors to stretch-stretch and zero out offsets. A common mistake is setting anchors incorrectly and wondering why an element doesn’t scale—anchors drive responsiveness, not just position. Try resizing the Game view while adjusting anchors to build intuition.

Anchors can be set to a single point or can stretch across the parent. When anchors are a single point—like top-left—the UI element’s Pos X and Pos Y are straight offsets from that anchor. This is ideal for placing a button in a corner with a fixed offset. When anchors stretch across an axis, the element resizes with the parent and Left/Right/Top/Bottom values act as padding. Use stretch anchors to create elements that track parent size, like a responsive background or a progress bar that scales. A concrete example: a health bar across the top should use left and right anchors stretched to both sides, with Top and Bottom offsets to set height. A common misconception is thinking anchors alone will center an element; you often also need to set pivot and Pos values. Another point: when you change anchor positions in the Scene view Unity can optionally keep the current apparent rectangle or update offsets—learn to use the anchored position vs world position presets to avoid unexpected jumps. Takeaway: choose point anchors for fixed offsets and stretch anchors for responsive sizing.

The pivot is the local origin point of a UI element’s Rect Transform and is expressed in normalized coordinates where (0,0) is bottom-left and (1,1) is top-right. Rotations and scaling occur around this pivot. For example, if you set the pivot to (0,1) — the top-left corner — and rotate the element, it will pivot around that corner instead of the center. Position and size fields change meaning depending on anchors: with point anchors, Pos X and Pos Y represent the offset from the anchor; with stretch anchors, the size is determined by the parent and Left/Right/Top/Bottom act like padding. A concrete lab example is making a button that grows from its center when hovered: set pivot to (0.5,0.5) and animate scale. A common mistake is rotating around an unexpected point because the pivot was left at a corner; always confirm pivot placement before animating. Closing thought: visualize the pivot like the hinge of a door — it tells you where rotations and scale originate and shapes how layout behaves.
